subtopic: 1.1.1 Structure and Function of the Processor
objectives: I can describe the roles of the ALU, Control Unit and the registers PC, MAR, MDR, CIR and ACC
I can trace the fetch-decode-execute cycle, naming every register transfer and bus involved
I can explain how clock speed, cores, cache and pipelining affect CPU performance, with caveats
I can compare Von Neumann, Harvard and contemporary (modified Harvard) architectures with distinct differences

retrieval.q: Convert the denary number 13 into 8-bit binary.
Convert the binary number 10110 into denary.
From GCSE: what is the overall job of the CPU in a computer system?
retrieval.a: It fetches, decodes and executes instructions, processing data and controlling the rest of the system.

retrieval.q: From GCSE: state one difference between RAM and ROM.
retrieval.a: RAM is volatile working memory that can be read and written; ROM is non-volatile and holds fixed startup instructions.

retrieval.q: From GCSE: what is an algorithm?
retrieval.a: A precise sequence of steps that solves a problem or completes a task.

keywords.def: Arithmetic Logic Unit; performs arithmetic, logic and shift operations, sending results to the accumulator.
Decodes instructions, generates control signals and synchronises the CPU using the clock.
Register holding the address of the next instruction to fetch; incremented every cycle.
Memory Address Register; holds the address of the memory location to be read from or written to.
Memory Data Register; holds the data or instruction just fetched from, or about to be written to, memory.
Current Instruction Register; holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
Small, very fast memory on or near the CPU holding frequently used data and instructions; not part of RAM.
Overlapping the fetch, decode and execute stages of consecutive instructions to raise throughput.
A single shared memory and bus for both data and instructions.

content.heading: The big picture: what the processor does
points: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it, then executes it
This loop is the fetch-decode-execute (FDE) cycle, running billions of times per second
Both instructions and data live in main memory as binary; the CPU cannot tell them apart by looking
Inside the CPU: the ALU, the Control Unit, and a set of registers
content.note: Everything this lesson builds on this one loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat.

content.heading: The ALU and the Control Unit
points: The ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide), logic (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons) and shifts
ALU results are placed in the accumulator (ACC)
The Control Unit decodes each instruction and generates control signals directing the other components
The CU manages the flow of data on the buses and synchronises everything with the clock

content.heading: The five special-purpose registers
points: A register is a tiny, extremely fast storage location inside the CPU
PC: address of the NEXT instruction; incremented each cycle
MAR: the address being read from or written to; MDR: the data or instruction itself
CIR: the current instruction while it is decoded and executed
ACC: the immediate result of ALU calculations
content.note: MAR holds an ADDRESS, MDR holds DATA. Swapping these is the most common lost mark.

content.heading: The three system buses
points: Address bus: carries addresses from CPU to memory; UNIDIRECTIONAL
Data bus: carries data and instructions between CPU and memory; bidirectional
Control bus: carries control signals such as read, write and clock; bidirectional
An address bus n bits wide can address 2^n memory locations

content.heading: FDE cycle: the fetch stage in full
points: The contents of the PC are copied into the MAR
A read signal is sent on the control bus; the instruction returns along the data bus into the MDR
The PC is incremented so it points at the following instruction
The instruction is copied from the MDR into the CIR
code: MDR = contents of memory at address in MAR
content.note: Candidates routinely miss the PC increment and the MDR to CIR copy — include both.

content.heading: FDE cycle: decode and execute
points: Decode: the CU splits the CIR contents into opcode (the operation) and operand (data or an address)
Execute an ALU operation: values are processed and the result goes to the ACC
Execute a load or store: data moves between memory and registers via MAR and MDR
Execute a jump or branch: a new address is written into the PC, changing what fetches next

content.heading: Performance factor 1: clock speed and cores
points: The clock sends regular pulses; speed in Hz is pulses per second
Higher clock speed means more FDE cycles per second, but heat and power consumption set a limit
A core is an independent processing unit running its own FDE cycle
More cores only help if the task can be split up AND the software supports multiple cores

content.heading: Performance factor 2: cache
points: Cache is small, very fast memory on or near the CPU holding frequently or recently used data
It is separate fast memory, NOT a section of RAM
Checked in order: L1 (smallest, fastest) then L2 then L3 (largest, slowest) then RAM
More cache means fewer slow trips to RAM, so the CPU waits less

content.heading: Performance factor 3: pipelining
points: Pipelining overlaps the fetch, decode and execute stages of consecutive instructions
While instruction 1 executes, instruction 2 decodes and instruction 3 is fetched
Throughput rises, but no individual instruction completes any faster
Jumps and branches cause hazards: prefetched instructions become wrong and must be flushed

content.heading: Von Neumann, Harvard and contemporary CPUs
points: Von Neumann: ONE shared memory and bus for data and instructions; simpler, cheaper, flexible; general-purpose PCs
Its weakness is the bottleneck: it cannot fetch an instruction and access data simultaneously
Harvard: SEPARATE memories and buses, allowing simultaneous instruction fetch and data access; costlier; embedded systems, microcontrollers, DSPs
Contemporary CPUs are modified (hybrid) Harvard: unified main memory but separate L1 instruction and data caches
content.note: This hybrid point IS spec bullet 1.1.1(e) — contemporary processor architecture.

worked_examples.title: Full register-transfer trace of fetching one instruction
steps: Suppose PC holds address 0052 and location 0052 contains the instruction ADD 13
Step 1: PC copied to MAR, so MAR now holds 0052
Step 2: read signal sent on the control bus; ADD 13 travels along the data bus into the MDR
Step 3: PC incremented, so PC now holds 0053
Step 4: MDR copied to CIR, so CIR now holds ADD 13
Decode: the CU splits ADD 13 into opcode ADD and operand 13
Execute: the value at address 13 is fetched (via MAR and MDR again), the ALU adds it to the ACC, and the result stays in the ACC

worked_examples.title: Address bus width calculation
steps: Question: a CPU has a 16-bit address bus. How many memory locations can it directly address?
Rule: an n-bit address bus addresses 2^n locations
Extension: widening the bus to 17 bits DOUBLES this to 131,072, because each extra bit doubles the address space
Common error: answering 16 x 2 or 2 x 16 instead of 2 to the power 16

worked_examples.title: Pipelining throughput: 6 instructions, 3 stages
steps: Without pipelining, each instruction needs 3 cycles (fetch, decode, execute) before the next starts: 6 x 3 = 18 cycles
With pipelining, a new instruction enters the pipeline every cycle once it is full
Cycle 1: I1 fetches. Cycle 2: I1 decodes, I2 fetches. Cycle 3: I1 executes, I2 decodes, I3 fetches
First instruction finishes at cycle 3; one more finishes every cycle after: cycles 3,4,5,6,7,8
Note: each instruction still takes 3 cycles of its own — latency is unchanged, throughput improves

activities.title: Living FDE Cycle (unplugged role-play)
instructions: Assign roles with labels: PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, CU, ALU, ACC, plus students at numbered desks as Memory holding instruction cards (LDA 12, ADD 13, STA 14, HLT)
Walk the fetch: PC shows their number to MAR; MAR calls the address down the one-way address bus; Memory hands the card to MDR via the data bus; PC increments; MDR passes the card to CIR
CU takes the card from CIR, splits it aloud into opcode and operand, and directs the execute: loads go via MDR to ACC; ADD sends both values to the ALU, who hands the result to ACC
Ban illegal moves: if data travels a route that does not exist (Memory talking straight to CIR, or Memory speaking back up the address bus), freeze and make the class spot it
Round 2: swap roles and include a branch instruction — the class must realise execute writes a new address into the PC
activities.stretch: Ask the branching PC-holder: what happens to the two instructions a pipeline would already have prefetched? (Flushed — branch hazard.)

activities.title: Human Pipeline Laundry Line
instructions: Set up three desks labelled FETCH, DECODE, EXECUTE; teacher claps to mark each clock cycle
Round 1, no pipelining: one instruction card at a time passes through all three desks before the next starts; class counts claps for 6 cards (18)
Round 2, pipelining: three volunteers, one per desk; every clap each desk passes its card forward and FETCH takes a new one; count again (8)
Ask: did any single instruction get faster? No — latency unchanged, throughput improved
Round 3: make card 3 a branch; when it executes, the cards in FETCH and DECODE are thrown away (pipeline flush) and the class recounts
activities.stretch: Instruction 4 needs the result of instruction 3, which has not executed yet — what are the CPU's options? (Stall, or predict/reorder.)

activities.title: Always-Sometimes-Never: CPU Performance
instructions: Display one statement at a time; pairs discuss for 30 seconds then show A, S or N on whiteboards simultaneously

Statements: doubling clock speed doubles program speed; a quad-core beats a dual-core; the address bus carries data to memory; a cache miss means fetching from RAM; increasing address bus width increases addressable memory; pipelining makes each instruction faster
Pick a pair from each camp to justify; every Sometimes must state when it is true and when false

Answers: Sometimes (bottlenecks, heat); Sometimes (only if parallelisable and software supports it); Never (addresses only, one-way); Sometimes (L2 or L3 may hit first); Always (2^n); Never (throughput rises, latency does not)
Close: pairs convert one Sometimes into an Always by adding the missing caveat
activities.stretch: Write one Sometimes statement about cache levels that would split the class.

practice.q: Describe the steps of the fetch phase of the fetch-decode-execute cycle, naming the registers and buses used. [4]
practice.a: The contents of the PC are copied into the MAR (1); a read signal is sent along the control bus and the instruction is transferred from memory along the data bus into the MDR (1); the PC is incremented to point to the next instruction (1); the instruction is copied from the MDR into the CIR (1).

practice.q: State the purpose of the MAR and the MDR. [2]
practice.a: The MAR holds the address of the memory location to be read from or written to (1); the MDR holds the data or instruction that has been fetched from, or is about to be written to, that location (1).

practice.q: Describe the role of the program counter, including what happens to it during a jump instruction. [3]
practice.a: The PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched (1); it is incremented during each fetch so it points to the following instruction (1); executing a jump writes a new address into the PC so execution continues from a different location (1).

practice.q: A CPU has a 24-bit address bus. Calculate the number of memory locations it can directly address. [2]
Explain why increasing the number of cores does not always make a program run faster. [3]
practice.a: The program or task may not be parallelisable, e.g. each step depends on the previous result (1); the software must be written to use multiple cores/threads, otherwise extra cores sit idle (1); coordinating and combining results between cores adds overhead, limiting the gain (1).

practice.q: Explain how cache improves the performance of the CPU. [3]
practice.a: Cache is small, very fast memory on or near the CPU (1); it stores frequently or recently used data and instructions (1); these can be accessed far faster than fetching from RAM, so the CPU spends less time waiting (1).

practice.q: Describe how pipelining increases the throughput of a processor and explain why a branch instruction reduces this benefit. [4]
practice.a: Pipelining overlaps the fetch, decode and execute stages of consecutive instructions (1), so one instruction can complete per clock cycle once the pipeline is full, raising throughput (1). A branch changes the PC to a new address (1), so the instructions already prefetched into the pipeline are wrong and must be flushed, wasting cycles (1).

practice.q: Compare Von Neumann and Harvard architectures, and state how contemporary processors combine the two. [6]
practice.a: Von Neumann has a single shared memory and bus for data and instructions (1) so it cannot fetch an instruction and access data simultaneously, causing a bottleneck (1), but is simpler/cheaper and used in general-purpose PCs (1). Harvard has separate memories and buses for data and instructions (1) allowing simultaneous access, and is used in embedded systems and DSPs (1). Contemporary CPUs are modified Harvard: unified main memory but separate L1 instruction and data caches (1).

misconceptions: Students often think the MAR holds data and the MDR holds addresses; it is the reverse — MAR is the ADDRESS register, MDR is the DATA register.
Students often think cache is a reserved section of RAM, but it is separate, much faster memory located on or near the CPU itself.
Students often think more cores always means proportionally faster, but the gain depends on the task being parallelisable and the software supporting it.
Students often think pipelining makes each instruction execute faster, but latency per instruction is unchanged; only throughput improves.
Students often think all three buses are two-way, but the address bus is unidirectional, carrying addresses from the CPU to memory only.
exam_link: Command words: State (1 mark definitions of registers), Describe (fetch stage, 3-4 marks), Explain (performance factors, 2-3 marks each), Compare/Discuss (architectures or buying advice, up to 9-mark levels of response).
The FDE trace is a classic 4-6 marker: marks are lost by omitting the PC increment and the MDR to CIR copy.

9-mark example stem: 'A gamer is choosing between a 3.2 GHz quad-core CPU with 8 MB cache and a 4.0 GHz dual-core with 2 MB cache. Discuss which is more suitable.' — answers must weigh clock, cores, cache AND the software caveat.
Calculation questions use 2^n for addressable locations; always show the power, not just the final value.
task: Write a full register-transfer trace for the two-instruction program LDA 20 then ADD 21, where address 20 holds 7 and address 21 holds 5. For each instruction give every fetch step (naming registers and buses), the decode split, and the execute action, finishing with the value left in the ACC (12).
challenge: A CPU has a 20-bit address bus and a 3-stage pipeline. Calculate the addressable locations (2^20 = 1,048,576), then calculate how many cycles 10 instructions take unpipelined (30) versus pipelined (12), and explain why a branch at instruction 5 would add wasted cycles.

exit_ticket.q: Name the two fetch-stage steps that candidates most often forget.
exit_ticket.a: Incrementing the PC, and copying the instruction from the MDR into the CIR.

exit_ticket.q: Which bus is unidirectional and what does it carry?
exit_ticket.a: The address bus; it carries memory addresses from the CPU to memory only.

exit_ticket.q: How do contemporary CPUs mix Von Neumann and Harvard designs?
exit_ticket.a: They use one unified main memory (Von Neumann) but separate L1 instruction and data caches (Harvard) — modified Harvard.
